items.text: SEASON 4 · EPISODE 6 · DRAFT  Truck · Maya, Cal and Lena · Level L3  A semifinal, live from a packed stadium on cellular only. The feed breaks every time the crowd roars. The engineer who walked out is in the truck — and so is his old mistake. And Maya’s.  ⚑ RV-92: capacity figures simplified. RV-93: invented schools and stadium. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Fourth Quarter
items.stakes: A semifinal, live from a packed stadium on cellular only. The man who walked out of master control is in the truck. He built tonight's presets.
items.reward: A feed that bends instead of breaking. A reporter who can talk. Maybe a truce with Cal.

objectives.text: Keep the feed alive in the crowd
Give the reporter a clean mix-minus
Ask about the slide on Lena's laptop
Look closer: two things in the truck

items.rumor: Cal's presets are in the truck. So is something on Lena's laptop she hasn't told anyone about.

items.alt: A packed stadium at night under lights, the crowd a sea of phone screens. A sideline reporter holds a microphone, earpiece in.
items.caption: Twenty thousand people. Twenty thousand phones. One bonded cellular kit.

items.alt: Inside the production truck: Cal at the encoder, headset on; Maya climbs in. They look at each other.
items.caption: The first time they've met.

lines.text: I'm the person reading your warnings.

items.prompt: Go on. Ask me why I walked out. Everyone else has.

options.label: “I don't need to know tonight. I need your presets explained.”
options.reply: …That's fair. Nobody's asked me to explain anything in two years.

options.label: “Tess ran the news alone because you left.”

items.alt: The truck door swings open between them. A stadium vendor leans in holding a tray of hot dogs. Cal and Maya stand at opposite ends of the truck, not looking at each other.

bubbles.text: Anybody want a hot dog? They're free. They're cold.

items.caption: The first thing they agree on.

items.text: 🔭 PHYSICS IN MOTION  Twenty thousand phones and four modems  The science under this episode’s problem — live.

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Cal and Maya beside a board. Shannon: C equals B times log-two of one plus S over N. B is bandwidth, S over N the signal-to-noise as a plain ratio. And the crowd pushes N up. So C comes down. Work out what's left.

bubbles.text: Shannon: C equals B times log-two of one plus S over N. B is bandwidth, S over N the signal-to-noise as a plain ratio.
And the crowd pushes N up.
So C comes down. Work out what's left.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Shannon limit   Bonded cellular   Adaptive bit rate   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Shannon capacity  C = B × log 2 (1 + S/N)   C  most data a channel can carry, bit/s  B  bandwidth, Hz  S/N  signal-to-noise ratio as a plain ratio (10 dB/10 )

items.alt: The bonded kit's status: four modems all with signal bars, each carrying only 2 to 3 Mb/s; the encoder fixed at 12 Mb/s, dropped three times.
items.caption: Every modem has bars. None of them has room.

items.title: “REMOTE 12M FIXED — C. (empty stadium)”
items.body: The words in brackets are the whole problem. Cal tuned it on a Tuesday afternoon with nobody in the stands. It's a perfect preset — for a stadium with no people in it.

items.prompt: 20:41. The feed just dropped for the third time. Fourth quarter in minutes. What do you do?
items.happening: Encoder fixed at 12 Mb/s; usable capacity ~11 and falling.
items.risk: The broadcast — and Lena's bet on cellular.
timeout: The feed drops a fourth time during a touchdown.
In a crowd, the fixed plan fails first.

options.label: Raise the bit rate to punch through
options.fail: Capacity is the limit, not effort.

options.label: Switch to adaptive bit rate with a 4 Mb/s floor and program prioritized
options.result: The picture softens a little. It stops dropping.
options.consequence: Viewers get a slightly softer game instead of a black screen. Cal watches you change his preset without a word.

options.label: Ask stadium operations to turn off the fan Wi-Fi
options.result: Stadium ops: “Twenty thousand people's Wi-Fi? No.”
options.consequence: Not yours to ask for — and it's not the bottleneck.
options.fail: The venue's network belongs to the venue; the phones are on cellular anyway.

options.label: Cut back to the studio for the rest of the game
options.consequence: The safe choice that cancels the job.

items.title: It isn't failing. It's full.
items.body: All four modems are healthy. The cells are shared with twenty thousand phones, and every link's capacity sank at kickoff. Cal's preset, tuned in an empty stadium, sends a fixed 12 Mb/s — it can't bend, so it breaks.
items.label: Test: which change helps most?

items.alt: The stands at a touchdown: thousands of phone screens rise at once to film the moment, a field of small white rectangles in the dark. The crowd roars.
narration: Every phone in the stadium rises to record the same six seconds. Every one of them takes a slice of the same cells.
items.caption: The best moment of the game is the worst moment for the link.

items.alt: System View: the encoder feeds four bonded modems, each carrying about 3.4 Mb/s usable in the crowd, into the station's receiver with a two-second buffer. The reporter's earpiece shows its source.
items.caption: Full, not failing.

items.label: **Learn it now:** contribution over cellular — bonding, buffering and bending.

items.alt: The sideline at halftime. The reporter presses her earpiece, frustrated. Maya on the radio.

bubbles.text: Every time I talk I hear myself two seconds later. I sound drunk.
What's in your ear right now?

items.alt: The truck's IFB panel: reporter's earpiece source is PROGRAM RETURN, latency 2.0 seconds, patched by C. Cal sees it.
items.caption: Program return, two seconds late, in the reporter's ear.

lines.text: Program return in her ear. That's… that's my patch.
I made the same one on a festival stage. A presenter cried.
(He doesn't say anything. He fixes his headset. It's the first time he's looked at her properly.)

items.title: The same mistake.
items.body: The reporter's earpiece is fed the program return from the station — the whole show, two seconds late through the cellular chain, including her own voice. It's exactly what Maya's template did to a presenter on a festival stage (S02E05). This time Cal built it.
items.label: Test: what does Maya do with that?
**Fix it:** give the reporter a clean mix-minus.

items.prompt: Halftime ends in three minutes. How do you prove her earpiece is right?
timeout: Test at the break or test on air.

options.label: Watch the IFB meter
options.result: Meters move. They moved before, too.
options.consequence: A meter can't hear an echo.
options.fail: The failure was a person hearing herself. Test that.

options.label: Ask the reporter to talk for a full minute with the truck live
Trust the patch — it's obviously right now
options.result: Second half: she stumbles once; a cue fader was still up.

options.label: Have Cal test it — it's his patch
options.result: Cal, quietly: “You test it. I'm too close to it.”

items.title: The limit of a channel
items.body: In 1948 Claude Shannon, at Bell Labs, published a mathematical theory of communication. It showed that every channel has a maximum rate for error-free information, set by its bandwidth and its signal-to-noise ratio. No clever encoder can beat it — which is why a stadium full of phones changes what a truck can send.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #37 · AVERY'S LENS  Bend, don't break  When conditions get worse, a system should degrade gracefully — lower quality before total failure — and tell people it's doing so.  The fixed 12 Mb/s preset couldn't bend. Adaptive with a floor looked a bit softer in the fourth quarter — and never went black.

items.alt: The second half, live: the reporter on camera, confident now, microphone up, earpiece in; a lower third reads Sideline, second half, live on bonded cellular.

bubbles.text: …and the Ridgebacks come out of the tunnel like they've got somewhere to be.

items.caption: No echo. Just her own voice, once.

items.alt: In the truck, Lena's laptop open on a slide: regional hub, nine stations, one master control; phase 1, Kestrel Valley; local engineering, zero. Maya sees it.
items.caption: Phase 1: Kestrel Valley. Local engineering: 0.

items.title: REGIONAL HUB · PHASE 1
items.body: A slide: *Nine stations. One master control, 400 km away. Phase 1: Kestrel Valley.* A second slide, half hidden: *Local engineering headcount: 0.* Cal sees Maya see it. He doesn't look surprised.

items.alt: Cal, beside Maya, looking at the same slide.

bubbles.text: That's why I stopped writing warnings. Nobody reads them when they've already decided.
Somebody's reading them now. I've crossed off five.

lines.text: Five. You were right about all of them.
(He says it like a man who knows one of them is about himself.)

items.prompt: After the game. You saw the hub slide. What do you do?
items.risk: Trust between Maya and Lena — and the station.
timeout: Lena closes the laptop and leaves. The question stays unasked.
Hard questions don't get easier with time.

options.label: Ask Lena directly, privately, tonight
options.result: Lena, tired: “Yes. The board wants it. I haven't decided. I wanted you to see the valley first.”
options.consequence: The truth, from its owner, before rumor.

options.label: Pretend you didn't see it
options.result: You carry it for four episodes.

options.label: Tell Tess and the crew
options.result: By Monday the newsroom thinks everyone's fired.
options.consequence: A rumor with your name on it.
options.fail: The owner should hear the question before the staff hears the rumor.

options.label: Confront Lena in front of the crew
options.consequence: She can't be honest in front of twelve people.
options.fail: Some conversations need a closed door.

items.label: **Route it:** stadium to living room — and back to her ear.
**Service Mode:** run the fourth quarter yourself.

items.alt: The stadium parking lot, late. Lena and Maya by the truck.

bubbles.text: The board wants the hub. I haven't decided. I wanted you to see the valley first.
I've seen the mountain, the river and a man who wrote fourteen warnings.

items.alt: Late, in the emptied truck. Cal coils a cable, over-under, loop after loop, without looking. Maya watches his hands.

bubbles.text: You coil like someone taught you.
Someone did. A long time ago. Across the valley.

narration: He doesn't say who. Maya has seen exactly one other person coil a cable like that.
items.caption: Over, under. The same hands, twenty years apart?

items.alt: Cal's warnings on the wall. Cal himself crosses out number ten, remote kit untested on cellular.
items.caption: Warning #10: crossed off — by Cal.

lines.text: (text) Second half: just me, no echo. I could have talked all night.
(reply) Please don't. It was a football game.

items.alt: Monday, 7:04 a.m. Maya in the station parking lot, phone to her ear, stopped mid-step.

bubbles.text: Sixty Aldermoor rooms went dark this morning. They all have addresses from your standard. Section 5.3.

items.caption: Next: *Section 5.3.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Plan remotes for the crowd, not the empty stadium: adaptive bit rate with a floor bends instead of breaking. A reporter's ear gets a mix-minus — never her own voice, never the late return — tested with her talking. And when you see a decision about people's jobs, ask the person who owns it.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Maya found her own old mistake in someone else's work and fixed it without a word of blame. Whose mistake have you recognized as your own?  Boundary: this reflection doesn't patch anything.
